CausalChain: DDR gene alterations in BTC -> Baseline accumulation of DNA damage and neoantigens -> Limited native immune activation due to immunosuppressive TME -> PARP inhibitor administration further induces DNA damage -> Increased cytosolic DNA and activation of the STING pathway -> Enhanced type I interferon response and antigen presentation -> Conversion of cold TME to hot TME -> Augmented efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Hypothesis: In biliary tract cancers harboring DDR alterations and an intermediate mutational landscape, the addition of PARP inhibitors to immune checkpoint blockade will enhance STING-mediated immune activation and antigen presentation, converting immunologically ‘cold’ tumors into ‘hot’ ones, thereby improving therapeutic response to immunotherapy.
Abstract: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) exhibit a heterogeneous molecular landscape where classical immunotherapy biomarkers such as PD‐L1 expression, MSI status, and tumor mutational burden (TMB) have shown limited predictive power. However, emerging evidence suggests that DNA damage repair (DDR) gene alterations, which are relatively frequent in BTCs, may modulate the tumor microenvironment (TME) by promoting neoantigen formation and stimulating innate immune signaling pathways. We propose that pharmacologically inducing additional DNA damage in BTCs with underlying DDR deficiencies through the use of PARP inhibitors may further enhance immunogenicity via activation of the STING pathway, thereby converting immunologically “cold” tumors into “hot” ones, and ultimately improving the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors. This hypothesis provides a new rationale for combined PARP inhibition and immunotherapy in a subset of BTCs characterized by intermediate TMB and capability for DDR‐associated immune activation.
